II23A-01.correct_answer: More eelgrass survived in Cadfield Cove than in Aldmoss Cove.
II23A-01.explanation: Achterberg blames "channel dredging," and Faulk blames "warm water discharged by the Elsby power plant instead." The channel "runs along the bay's eastern shore" and the discharge reaches "only" the "northern shore," so Aldmoss Cove ("in the northeast") gets both, Cadfield Cove ("in the northwest") gets only the discharge, Brackwell Cove ("in the southeast") gets only the dredging, and Dellow Cove ("in the southwest") gets neither. The finding that "More eelgrass survived in Cadfield Cove than in Aldmoss Cove." means Aldmoss thinned more than Cadfield; both receive the discharge and only Aldmoss is beside the channel, so the difference isolates dredging and supports Achterberg. The finding that "More eelgrass survived in Dellow Cove than in Aldmoss Cove." sets the cove with both factors against the cove with neither, so both accounts predict it. The finding that "More eelgrass survived in Dellow Cove than in Cadfield Cove." means Cadfield thinned more than Dellow; neither is beside the channel, so it supports Faulk and says nothing about dredging. The finding that "More eelgrass survived in Brackwell Cove than in Dellow Cove." means the cove with neither factor thinned more than Brackwell, which is beside the channel, so it weakens Achterberg's hypothesis.

II23A-02.correct_answer: Salamanders from Corlett weighed less than salamanders from Ambersley.
II23A-02.explanation: Brevard attributes the decline "mainly to invasive earthworms," and Elling "mainly to logging." Corlett "was logged recently, but earthworms have not reached it," while earthworms "now fill Ambersley," which is "unlogged," and both lie on "level valley ground." The finding that "Salamanders from Corlett weighed less than salamanders from Ambersley." therefore shows the logged, worm-free stand faring worse than the worm-filled, unlogged one on the same kind of ground, the opposite of what Brevard's hypothesis predicts, so it most directly weakens it. The finding that "Salamanders from Dace Ridge weighed less than salamanders from Ambersley." also has a worm-free stand lighter than Ambersley, but Dace Ridge is "a steep and sunny slope," and both agree that salamanders "on steep, sun-baked slopes weigh less than those on level ground," so the slope could explain it. The finding that "Salamanders from Ambersley weighed less than salamanders from Fenwold." compares two unlogged level stands that differ only in earthworms, with the worm-filled one lighter, so it supports Brevard. The finding that "Salamanders from Fenwold weighed less than salamanders from Corlett." compares two worm-free level stands that differ only in logging, with the unlogged one lighter; it weakens Elling's account, not Brevard's.

II23A-03.correct_answer: Coppling plants in the rural garden flowered earlier than Dinsmore plants in the rural garden.
II23A-03.explanation: Dalgren holds that "city populations have evolved to flower early," while Corby holds that "the warmth of cities simply speeds the plants along." "Coppling seeds came from a city lot and Dinsmore seeds from a rural meadow, and both were of ordinary weight," so plants from the two sources grown side by side in the same garden differ only in origin. The finding that "Coppling plants in the rural garden flowered earlier than Dinsmore plants in the rural garden." shows city-origin plants flowering first without any city warmth, which supports Dalgren. The finding that "Esterholm plants in the rural garden flowered earlier than Dinsmore plants in the rural garden." also compares city-origin and rural plants in the same garden, but "Esterholm seeds ... were unusually heavy," and both agree that "plants grown from unusually heavy seeds tend to flower sooner," so seed weight could explain it. The finding that "Coppling plants in the city garden flowered earlier than Dinsmore plants in the rural garden." gives the city-origin plants the warm garden as well, so both accounts predict it. The finding that "Dinsmore plants in the city garden flowered earlier than Coppling plants in the city garden." has rural-origin plants flowering before city-origin plants in the same garden, which weakens Dalgren's hypothesis.

II23A-04.correct_answer: More of the oak seedlings survived in the Daleford tract in 2006 than in the Carbery tract in 2006.
II23A-04.explanation: Abernell "credits deer fences," while Cole "credits prescribed burns instead." From 2000 on, the Carbery tract was fenced and no longer burned ("Fences went up around the Carbery tract in 2000, when the burning it had received through the 1990s ended"), while the Daleford tract was burned but "never fenced." In the same year, the finding that "More of the oak seedlings survived in the Daleford tract in 2006 than in the Carbery tract in 2006." shows the burned, unfenced tract outdoing the fenced, unburned one, the opposite of what Abernell's hypothesis predicts, so it most directly weakens it. The finding that "More of the oak seedlings survived in the Carbery tract in 2004 than in the Carbery tract in 1997." compares the Carbery tract when fenced with the same tract when it was only burned; both years fall before 2010, when survival "was otherwise steady from year to year," so it supports Abernell. The finding that "More of the oak seedlings survived in the Daleford tract in 2012 than in the Carbery tract in 2007." also has Daleford ahead, but 2012 falls in "the run of wet summers that began in 2010" and 2007 does not, so the weather could explain it. The finding that "More of the oak seedlings survived in the Daleford tract in 2013 than in the Eldwick tract in 2013." compares two unfenced tracts in the same year that differ only in burning, so it supports Cole and says nothing against fences.

II23A-05.correct_answer: Colonies at Bramel stored less honey than colonies at Ardane.
II23A-05.explanation: Fenn holds that "the heavier an apiary's infestation, the less honey its colonies store," while Dacosta blames "pesticide drifting from sprayed orchards." Bramel, a lowland apiary not among those that "border sprayed orchards," had 7 mites per 100 bees, while Ardane, also in the lowlands, borders orchards and had only 3. The finding that "Colonies at Bramel stored less honey than colonies at Ardane." therefore has the more heavily infested, unsprayed apiary doing worse than the lightly infested, sprayed one at the same elevation, which supports Fenn over Dacosta. The finding that "Colonies at Cromby stored less honey than colonies at Ardane." also has a heavily infested, unsprayed apiary doing worse than Ardane, but "Cromby is the only one in the uplands," and both agree "that colonies at high elevation tend to store less honey," so elevation could explain it. The finding that "Colonies at Ardane stored less honey than colonies at Dunholt." compares two lowland apiaries with the same load of 3 mites that differ only in orchard spray, so it supports Dacosta and says nothing about mites. The finding that "Colonies at Ardane stored less honey than colonies at Elvey." compares two lowland apiaries that both border orchards, and the one with fewer mites (Ardane, 3, against Elvey, 5) stored less, which weakens Fenn's hypothesis.

II23A-06.correct_answer: On Benvoray, the colony raised 273 chicks from 420 nests.
II23A-06.explanation: Faye argues that "on at least one island with more than 5 rats per hectare, the colony raised more than 0.6 chicks per nest." Benvoray holds an estimated 310 rats on 50 hectares, or 6.2 per hectare, and "On Benvoray, the colony raised 273 chicks from 420 nests." works out to 0.65 chicks per nest, so it meets both conditions. "On Ardvane, the colony raised 146 chicks from 200 nests." gives the best rate of the four, 0.73 chicks per nest, but Ardvane's 168 rats on 42 hectares come to only 4.0 per hectare, not more than 5. "On Dunvarra, the colony raised 487 chicks from 880 nests." is the largest number of chicks, and Dunvarra has 6.0 rats per hectare (540 on 90), but 487 chicks from 880 nests is only about 0.55 per nest. "On Caillin, the colony raised 341 chicks from 590 nests." comes from an island with 7.0 rats per hectare (238 on 34), but 341 chicks from 590 nests is about 0.58 per nest, just short of 0.6. All four choices read the table accurately.

II23A-07.correct_answer: the smaller barnacle numbered 33 per 100 cm² at Dovell, compared with 17 at Brockel.
II23A-07.explanation: The larger species "cannot survive more than 1.1 meters above the low-tide line," and heights were recorded "from a survey bolt set 0.4 meter below that line," so the limit lies 1.5 meters above the bolt in the table. Dovell (1.7 meters) is above the limit and Brockel (1.0 meter) below it, so "the smaller barnacle numbered 33 per 100 cm² at Dovell, compared with 17 at Brockel." shows a site above the limit more crowded than one below it, as Brack claims. "the smaller barnacle numbered 38 per 100 cm² at Cendry, compared with 17 at Brockel." shows the largest density, and Cendry (1.3 meters) is higher than Brockel, but 1.3 meters above the bolt is only 0.9 meter above the low-tide line, so both sites are below the limit. "the smaller barnacle numbered 17 per 100 cm² at Brockel, compared with 11 at Fenlow." does compare a site below the limit (Brockel) with one above it (Fenlow, 2.4 meters), but the lower site is the more crowded one, the opposite of the claim. "the smaller barnacle numbered 24 per 100 cm² at Eskett, compared with 11 at Fenlow." compares Eskett (2.1 meters) and Fenlow (2.4 meters), both above the limit, and the lower of the two is more crowded, so it bears on neither part of the claim.

II23A-08.correct_answer: Copperhill set fruit on 50% of its flowers at 35°C and ripened its first fruit in 66 days.
II23A-08.explanation: Faircloth required that fruit set "fall by no more than 10 percentage points between 25°C and 35°C" and that the variety "ripen its first fruit sooner than Amberlee does"; the table gives Amberlee 71 days. "Copperhill set fruit on 50% of its flowers at 35°C and ripened its first fruit in 66 days." describes a variety that ripens in 66 days, sooner than 71, and whose fruit set falls from 58% at 25°C to 50%, a drop of 8 points, so it meets both requirements. "Birchtop set fruit on 60% of its flowers at 35°C and ripened its first fruit in 64 days." ripens in 64 days, but Birchtop's fruit set falls from 73% to 60%, a drop of 13 points. "Emberglow set fruit on 68% of its flowers at 35°C and ripened its first fruit in 76 days." has the highest fruit set at 35°C, and its drop is only 8 points (76% to 68%), but at 76 days it ripens later than Amberlee. "Dawnlight set fruit on 55% of its flowers at 35°C and ripened its first fruit in 74 days." drops only 7 points (62% to 55%), but at 74 days it also ripens later than Amberlee. All four choices read the table accurately.

II23B-01.correct_answer: More sinkholes opened in Ingold over the past decade than in Harrowfield.
II23B-01.explanation: Granlund blames "leaking water mains"; Ivers blames the quarry's pumping. Ingold "still has its original cast-iron mains, which leak badly" and sits "on thick soil far from the quarry," while Harrowfield, also "on thick soil," "has new plastic pipe but lies beside the quarry." With soil thickness equal, Ingold has only leaking mains and Harrowfield has only the quarry, so "More sinkholes opened in Ingold over the past decade than in Harrowfield" favors Granlund's account over Ivers's and most directly supports it. "More sinkholes opened in Lammert over the past decade than in Harrowfield" also sets leaking mains against the quarry, but Lammert is "on thin soil," and both researchers agree that sinkholes "open more readily wherever the soil over the limestone is thin," so the soil could explain the result. "More sinkholes opened in Lammert over the past decade than in Ingold" compares two districts that both have leaking mains and neither of which is near the quarry; both accounts expect thin-soiled Lammert to fare worse. "More sinkholes opened in Jorvenn over the past decade than in Ingold" would weaken Granlund's hypothesis, since Jorvenn, with sealed pipe, would outdo Ingold, which differs from it only in its leaking mains.

II23B-02.correct_answer: The ice broke up later in spring on Hamrin than on Isel.
II23B-02.explanation: Hovik credits "meltwater from glaciers"; Kalland credits "the shadow of cliffs." Hamrin still receives glacial meltwater but lies "in open basins," while Isel's glacier has "vanished" and "Steep cliffs shade the ice on Isel." The finding that "The ice broke up later in spring on Hamrin than on Isel" therefore has the lake with only meltwater outlasting the lake with only shade, which supports Hovik over Kalland. "The ice broke up later in spring on Kjelda than on Hamrin" compares two lakes that both receive meltwater; Kjelda differs only in being shaded, so the finding supports Kalland. "The ice broke up later in spring on Kjelda than on Garma" compares a lake with both meltwater and shade against an open lake with no glacier, so both accounts predict it. "The ice broke up later in spring on Isel than on Kjelda" compares two shaded lakes that differ only in that Kjelda receives meltwater, so it would weaken Hovik's hypothesis.

II23B-03.correct_answer: Seismometers recorded more small earthquakes in Gisler in 2017 than in Kvamby in 2015.
II23B-03.explanation: Lagerholm blames wastewater injection, which "began in Gisler, Hollis, and Jessenby in 2012"; Gerhardsen blames hydraulic fracturing, which "began in Hollis and Kvamby in 2014." "Gisler has never been fracked, and Kvamby has never received injected wastewater," and neither is described as sitting on the fault zone. In 2017 Gisler had injection only, and in 2015 Kvamby had fracturing only; since earthquake counts otherwise "change little from year to year," "Seismometers recorded more small earthquakes in Gisler in 2017 than in Kvamby in 2015" sets injection alone against fracturing alone and most directly supports Lagerholm. "Seismometers recorded more small earthquakes in Jessenby in 2016 than in Kvamby in 2017" also sets an injection district against a fracturing district, but Jessenby "sits on an old fault zone" and has more earthquakes "by itself," so the fault could explain the result. "Seismometers recorded more small earthquakes in Hollis in 2016 than in Gisler in 2010" compares a district with both injection and fracturing against a district that in 2010 had neither, so both accounts predict it. "Seismometers recorded more small earthquakes in Gisler in 2011 than in Gisler in 2015" would weaken Lagerholm's hypothesis, since Gisler had fewer earthquakes after injection began than before.

II23B-04.correct_answer: Kvist lost less soil over the study period than Gorrel did.
II23B-04.explanation: Kalvik predicts that "the more hikers a trail carries, the faster it wears down"; Hennum blames horses. Kvist carries "about 300 hikers a day" and Gorrel "about 120," neither is open to horses (riders "are barred from Kvist," and Ingle, "unlike Gorrel, is open to horses"), and both cross "gentle ground." They differ only in foot traffic, so "Kvist lost less soil over the study period than Gorrel did" has the busier trail wearing less, which most directly weakens Kalvik's hypothesis. "Kvist lost less soil over the study period than Ingle did" also has the busier trail losing less, but Ingle carries horses and "climbs a slope twice as steep," and both researchers agree a steeper trail "loses more soil by itself," so the slope could explain the result. "Gorrel lost less soil over the study period than Halder did" sets a quieter trail without horses against a busier trail with horses, so both accounts predict it. "Halder lost less soil over the study period than Kvist did" compares two trails with the same 300 hikers that differ only in horses, so it weakens Hennum's account, not Kalvik's.

II23B-05.correct_answer: Water from the Kelstad well in 2022 contained more salt than water from the Gullhaven well in 2018.
II23B-05.explanation: Hagelin blames seawater seeping inland "steadily and for decades," which would affect only coastal Gullhaven; Laukvik blames irrigation water, which farms around Kelstad "began drawing from a brackish canal in 2020." In 2022 Kelstad had irrigation but no seawater, and Gullhaven had seawater but no irrigation in any year; neither well passes through the clay at Ljorn. Because the seepage is steady, the year of the Gullhaven sample does not matter, so "Water from the Kelstad well in 2022 contained more salt than water from the Gullhaven well in 2018" has irrigation alone outdoing seawater alone, which most directly weakens Hagelin's hypothesis. "Water from the Ljorn well in 2022 contained more salt than water from the Gullhaven well in 2022" also has an inland well outdoing the coastal one, but Ljorn's "layer of salty marine clay" "by itself makes its water saltier," so the clay could explain the result. "Water from the Gullhaven well in 2018 contained more salt than water from the Kelstad well in 2018" sets the coastal well against an inland well in a year before its farms began irrigating, so it supports Hagelin. "Water from the Ljorn well in 2022 contained more salt than water from the Kelstad well in 2018" compares two inland wells, neither of them irrigated (Kelstad in 2018 had not yet begun); both accounts expect the clay well to be saltier, whatever the year.

II23B-06.correct_answer: The Ivesk well was pumped at 18.0 liters per second, lowering its water level by 8.0 meters.
II23B-06.explanation: Larsgard's claim needs a well "deeper than 80 meters" whose specific capacity "exceeded 2 liters per second for each meter of drawdown." The table gives Ivesk a depth of 95 meters, and 18.0 liters per second over 8.0 meters of drawdown is 2.25 liters per second per meter, so "The Ivesk well was pumped at 18.0 liters per second, lowering its water level by 8.0 meters" completes the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. "The Grinde well was pumped at 9.0 liters per second, lowering its water level by 4.2 meters" gives about 2.14 liters per second per meter, above 2, but Grinde is only 60 meters deep. "The Hallum well was pumped at 12.0 liters per second, lowering its water level by 6.2 meters" describes a 110-meter well, but its specific capacity is about 1.94, just short of 2. "The Jaren well was pumped at 6.0 liters per second, lowering its water level by 3.6 meters" describes an 88-meter well whose specific capacity is about 1.67.

II23B-07.correct_answer: Flow at Iskilde rose from 30 liters per second in 2005 to 38 liters per second in 2020.
II23B-07.explanation: Haraldsen's claim needs a spring "whose flow fell between 1990 and 2005" and whose flow then "rose by more than 20 percent from 2005 to 2020." The table shows Iskilde falling from 41 to 30 liters per second between 1990 and 2005, and a rise from 30 to 38 is about 27 percent, so "Flow at Iskilde rose from 30 liters per second in 2005 to 38 liters per second in 2020" completes the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. "Flow at Granberg rose from 45 liters per second in 2005 to 56 liters per second in 2020" is a rise of about 24 percent, but Granberg's flow went up, from 40 to 45, between 1990 and 2005, so it is not a spring that had weakened. "Flow at Ludal rose from 80 liters per second in 2005 to 92 liters per second in 2020" describes a spring that did fall (from 95) and the largest gain in liters per second, but 12 on 80 is a rise of only 15 percent. "Flow at Hjelset rose from 22 liters per second in 2005 to 25 liters per second in 2020" is a rise of about 14 percent, and Hjelset's flow had risen, not fallen, before 2005.

II23B-08.correct_answer: On Jassel, hydrated minerals made up 3.4% of the surface, compared with 1.6% on Gyllen.
II23B-08.explanation: Haugen classes an asteroid as beyond the snow line "only if even its closest approach to the sun lies beyond 2.7 AU," and claims one beyond the line "can carry at least twice the share of hydrated minerals of one inside it." Jassel's closest approach is 2.85 AU, so it is beyond the line, while Gyllen never goes past 2.55 AU; 3.4% is more than twice 1.6%, so "On Jassel, hydrated minerals made up 3.4% of the surface, compared with 1.6% on Gyllen" completes the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. "On Lisvold, hydrated minerals made up 3.8% of the surface, compared with 1.6% on Gyllen" also shows more than a doubling, and Lisvold's orbit reaches 3.10 AU, but its closest approach is 2.40 AU, so under Haugen's rule both asteroids are inside the line. "On Kolbeck, hydrated minerals made up 6.3% of the surface, compared with 3.5% on Hennick" does pair an asteroid beyond the line (closest approach 2.95 AU) with one inside it, but 6.3% is less than twice 3.5%. "On Ivra, hydrated minerals made up 8.2% of the surface, compared with 6.3% on Kolbeck" runs the wrong way: Ivra's closest approach is 2.55 AU, so the richer asteroid is the one inside the line.

II23C-01.correct_answer: Residents of Nettleford commuted by bicycle more often than residents of Mossgate did.
II23C-01.explanation: Pazos holds that "protected bike lanes are what draw commuters onto bicycles," while Ruddock "contends instead that bike-share stations" are decisive. Mossgate and Nettleford both lie on the plain, where "Mossgate has 12 kilometers of lanes but no stations, and Nettleford has stations but no lanes." If "Residents of Nettleford commuted by bicycle more often than residents of Mossgate did," then an equally flat district with stations and no lanes outdid the district with the most lanes, the reverse of what Pazos predicts and just what Ruddock predicts, so this most directly weakens her hypothesis. "Residents of Pellam commuted by bicycle more often than residents of Orrinby did" also sets a district without lanes ahead of one with 12 kilometers of them, but Orrinby is on the ridge and Pellam on the plain, and both accept "that steep streets discourage cycling whatever a district offers," so the slope could explain the gap. "Residents of Quenby commuted by bicycle more often than residents of Ramsell did" compares two ridge districts, but Quenby has both lanes and stations and Ramsell "has neither," so both accounts expect it. "Residents of Pellam commuted by bicycle more often than residents of Nettleford did" compares two plain districts without lanes that differ only in stations; it weakens Ruddock's account, not Pazos's.

II23C-02.correct_answer: There was less car traffic in Mellick on weekdays than in Pasterby on weekdays.
II23C-02.explanation: Renshaw credits congestion charges, and Ormsby "credits bus lanes instead." On weekdays Mellick charges drivers and Pasterby, which "charges drivers only on weekends and has no bus lanes," does not; both are rail towns and neither runs bus lanes. So "There was less car traffic in Mellick on weekdays than in Pasterby on weekdays" compares two towns that differ only in the charge, and it most directly supports Renshaw. "There was less car traffic in Mellick on weekdays than in Norrance on weekdays" looks like a direct contest between a charge and bus lanes, since Norrance "runs bus lanes on weekdays," but Mellick is on a rail line and Norrance is not, and both agree that "a town on a rail line carries less car traffic," so the railway could explain it. "There was less car traffic in Mellick on weekends than in Pasterby on weekends" compares two rail towns without bus lanes on a day when only Pasterby charges, and the uncharged town has less traffic, which weakens Renshaw. "There was less car traffic in Mellick on weekends than in Norrance on weekends" also has the uncharged town ahead, since "Norrance also charges only on weekends," so it cannot support Renshaw, and the railway could explain it in any case.

II23C-03.correct_answer: Residents of Nethercote could name more of their neighbors than residents of Quellin could.
II23C-03.explanation: Marchand credits front porches, while Nakagawa "contends instead that what matters is the cul-de-sac." Nethercote is a Rennard development, so its houses have porches, and because it was "finished in 1992," before the 1994 rule, its streets run through. Quellin is Mabley's, so it has no porches, and it was begun "before" the rule, so it too lacks cul-de-sacs. "Residents of Nethercote could name more of their neighbors than residents of Quellin could" therefore holds street layout constant and varies only porches, which most directly supports Marchand. "Residents of Morwen could name more of their neighbors than residents of Quellin could" is expected under both accounts, because Morwen is a Rennard development "begun after the rule took effect" and so has both porches and cul-de-sacs, while Quellin has neither. "Residents of Ottersby could name more of their neighbors than residents of Nethercote could" favors Ottersby, a Mabley development with cul-de-sacs, over the porch neighborhood without them, which supports Nakagawa. "Residents of Ottersby could name more of their neighbors than residents of Morwen could" compares two cul-de-sac neighborhoods of which only Morwen has porches, and the porch neighborhood does worse, which weakens Marchand.

II23C-04.correct_answer: Farms around Ruskett adopted the variety earlier than farms around Merrigal did.
II23C-04.explanation: Okoro credits extension offices, and Pemberton "argues instead that access to credit was decisive." Merrigal has an extension office and no bank branch, Ruskett "has neither," and both "stand beside the valley's market town." So "Farms around Ruskett adopted the variety earlier than farms around Merrigal did" compares two places equally close to market, both without a bank, that differ only in the extension office; the place without the office adopted first, which most directly weakens Okoro's hypothesis. "Farms around Ruskett adopted the variety earlier than farms around Nolby did" also puts Ruskett ahead of a place the office serves, but Nolby is "a hamlet two days' travel up the valley," and both note that "farms far from a market, where seed is sold, tend to take up new crops later," so distance could explain the result. "Farms around Merrigal adopted the variety earlier than farms around Prandle did" puts the place with an extension office ahead of the place with a bank, which supports Okoro. "Farms around Prandle adopted the variety earlier than farms around Ruskett did" compares places that differ only in having a bank branch, so it supports Pemberton and says nothing against Okoro.

II23C-05.correct_answer: Residents of Quorley spent less on sugary drinks in 2017 than residents of Mistlow did in 2017.
II23C-05.explanation: Ramsden credits the tax, while Quarrie suspects "an advertising campaign warning about sugar." In 2017 Quorley, which "began taxing sugary drinks in 2016," had the tax, and it "has never run the campaign"; Mistlow, "which has no tax, adopted it only in 2019," so in 2017 it had neither. "Residents of Quorley spent less on sugary drinks in 2017 than residents of Mistlow did in 2017" therefore compares two towns in the same year that differ only in the tax, which most directly supports Ramsden. "Residents of Pendry spent less on sugary drinks in 2017 than residents of Ravelle did in 2017" looks like a taxed town beating an untouched one, but Pendry's tax began only "in 2019"; in 2017 Pendry had only the campaign, "which Pendry launched in 2016," so the finding supports Quarrie. "Residents of Pendry spent less on sugary drinks in 2021 than residents of Pendry did in 2017" is tempting because Pendry gained the tax between those years, but spending "had been falling across the Ombrey region for years," so the drop could have happened without the tax. "Residents of Ravelle spent less on sugary drinks in 2021 than residents of Quorley did in 2021" has the untaxed town ahead of the taxed one, with no campaign in either, which weakens Ramsden.

II23C-06.correct_answer: the Moxley station sold 55,000 gallons a week, compared with 42,000 at the Rindell station.
II23C-06.explanation: The road "reaches the county line 4 kilometers beyond the bridge," so a station is outside the county only if it lies more than 4 kilometers east of the bridge. Moxley, 6 kilometers east, is outside, and Rindell, 1 kilometer east, is still inside, so "the Moxley station sold 55,000 gallons a week, compared with 42,000 at the Rindell station" shows a station just past the line outselling one nearer the city. All four choices read the table accurately. "the Rindell station sold 42,000 gallons a week, compared with 38,000 at the Nydell station" shows a farther station outselling a nearer one, and the two lie on opposite sides of the bridge, but both are inside the county (1 kilometer east and 3 kilometers west of the bridge), so the tax cannot explain it. "the Padstone station sold 49,000 gallons a week, compared with 33,000 at the Oberwick station" compares a station inside the county (3 kilometers east of the bridge) with one outside it (11 kilometers), but the station inside sells more, the opposite of the claim. "the Quelling station sold 64,000 gallons a week, compared with 55,000 at the Moxley station" has the largest figure, but Quelling, west of the bridge, is inside the county and Moxley is outside, so it too shows the nearer, taxed station selling more.

II23C-07.correct_answer: Mavisford's store sold 33,300 books in a year, and the town has 9,000 residents.
II23C-07.explanation: The fund requires a store to sell "more than three books per resident each year," and Montague's claim concerns "a store more than 40 kilometers from the nearest college." Mavisford is 52 kilometers from the nearest college, and 33,300 books for 9,000 residents is 3.7 books per resident, so "Mavisford's store sold 33,300 books in a year, and the town has 9,000 residents" completes the text. All four choices read the table accurately. "Ollerby's store sold 13,200 books in a year, and the town has 4,000 residents" clears the bar at 3.3 books per resident, but the table puts Ollerby only 18 kilometers from a college. "Pembray's store sold 28,200 books in a year, and the town has 9,600 residents" concerns a town 61 kilometers from a college, but 28,200 divided by 9,600 is about 2.94, just short of three. "Quintard's store sold 27,300 books in a year, and the town has 10,500 residents" concerns a town 45 kilometers from a college, but its sales come to only 2.6 books per resident.

II23C-08.correct_answer: Quillow's course graduated 36 students, who went on to earn $21.60 an hour.
II23C-08.explanation: A course qualifies only if graduates "earn at least $4.00 more per hour after the course than they did before it" and "at least 75 percent of enrollees must finish." Quillow's 36 graduates came from 44 enrollees, about 82 percent, and their wage rose from $17.40 to $21.60, a gain of $4.20, so "Quillow's course graduated 36 students, who went on to earn $21.60 an hour" identifies the one course meeting both conditions. All four choices read the table accurately. "Nanbury's course graduated 26 students, who went on to earn $20.30 an hour" describes a wage gain of $4.50 (from $15.80), but 26 of 40 enrollees is only 65 percent. "Prestley's course graduated 20 students, who went on to earn $18.80 an hour" describes a course that 20 of 24 enrollees, about 83 percent, finished, but the gain from $14.90 is $3.90, just under $4.00. "Orwen's course graduated 31 students, who went on to earn $20.15 an hour" fails both conditions: 31 of 45 is about 69 percent, and the gain from $16.60 is $3.55.

II23D-01.correct_answer: More ballad sheets per household were sold in Sellwick in 1835 than in Sellwick in 1845.
II23D-01.explanation: Vollmer hypothesizes that "railways raised these sales." Sellwick got its railway in 1840 and "held no market and had no free school," so Sellwick in 1835 and Sellwick in 1845 differ only in the railway. The finding that "More ballad sheets per household were sold in Sellwick in 1835 than in Sellwick in 1845" shows sales falling after the railway arrived with nothing else changed, which most directly weakens Vollmer's hypothesis. The finding that "More ballad sheets per household were sold in Ulsby in 1845 than in Wrexley in 1845" has a school town without a railway outselling a railway town in the same year, but Ulsby is a market town and Wrexley is not, and both historians accept that market towns "sold more ballads than other towns whatever their schools or railways," so the market could explain it. The finding that "More ballad sheets per household were sold in Wrexley in 1845 than in Sellwick in 1835" compares Wrexley after its railway arrived with Sellwick before its railway arrived; neither had a market or a school, so it supports Vollmer. The finding that "More ballad sheets per household were sold in Thaxford in 1845 than in Wrexley in 1835" compares two towns that, at those dates, had neither a railway nor a school; only Thaxford's market differs, which both historians expect to raise sales.

II23D-02.correct_answer: Brides in Stavely signed their names more often than brides in Tessaby did.
II23D-02.explanation: Yarde ties signing to "the number of years a parish had employed a schoolmaster," while Sjoberg ties it to the turnpike road. Stavely, "an upland parish off the road," had a schoolmaster for forty years; Tessaby, "an upland parish on the road, never had one." Both are upland parishes, so the finding that "Brides in Stavely signed their names more often than brides in Tessaby did" has the schooled parish winning even though only the other parish had the road, which most directly supports Yarde. The finding that "Brides in Wrayburn signed their names more often than brides in Tessaby did" also sets a schooled parish off the road against Tessaby, but Wrayburn is a valley parish, and both scholars accept that "valley parishes, being richer, had more signers than upland ones," so wealth could explain it. The finding that "Brides in Vintrell signed their names more often than brides in Wrayburn did" favors the parish with more years of schooling, but Vintrell was also on the road and Wrayburn was not, so both accounts predict it. The finding that "Brides in Upthorne signed their names more often than brides in Sutterby did" compares two road parishes that never had a schoolmaster; only valley against upland differs.

II23D-03.correct_answer: Less property per household was lost to fire in Sallowby than in Vexley.
II23D-03.explanation: Ulvang credits "a paid fire company equipped with hand pumps"; Zell credits an ordinance "requiring tile rather than thatch on roofs." Sallowby kept a fire company without the ordinance, and Vexley passed the ordinance without a fire company; both lie on the exposed headland. The finding that "Less property per household was lost to fire in Sallowby than in Vexley" therefore holds exposure equal and shows the fire-company town doing better than the ordinance town, which most directly supports Ulvang and runs against Zell. The finding that "Less property per household was lost to fire in Skelby than in Vexley" sets a fire-company town against the same ordinance town, but Skelby lies on the sheltered harbor, and both historians accept that fire "spread farther in the towns on the exposed headland," so shelter could explain it. The finding that "Less property per household was lost to fire in Ulverholm than in Sallowby" has a town with no defenses doing better, but Ulverholm is a harbor town and Sallowby a headland town, so exposure explains it and it says little about the fire company. The finding that "Less property per household was lost to fire in Yarlow than in Sallowby" compares two headland towns, neither with the ordinance, that differ only in the fire company, and the town without one did better, which weakens Ulvang's hypothesis.

II23D-04.correct_answer: Children in Tenlow left school later in 1851 than children in Sudmere did in 1851.
II23D-04.explanation: Tennant credits school boards "requiring attendance to the age of twelve"; Vasquez credits mills that "refused to hire anyone under thirteen." Sudmere had a school board, and its mills hired children of any age; Tenlow had the mill rule but "no school board." The finding that "Children in Tenlow left school later in 1851 than children in Sudmere did in 1851" compares the two towns in the same year and shows the town without a school board keeping children longer, which most directly weakens Tennant's hypothesis. The finding that "Children in Tenlow left school later in 1858 than children in Sudmere did in 1851" sets the same towns against each other, but the Tenlow figure comes from 1858, "a year of deep trade slump" that "kept children in school longer everywhere," so the slump could explain it. The finding that "Children in Sudmere left school later in 1858 than children in Verrow did in 1858" compares two towns whose mills hired children of any age, in the same year, and the town with a school board kept children longer, which supports Tennant. The finding that "Children in Verrow left school later in 1851 than children in Tenlow did in 1851" compares two towns without school boards that differ only in the mill rule, so it weakens Vasquez's account, not Tennant's.

II23D-05.correct_answer: More clerks' households in Sarnby owned a piano than shopkeepers' households in Sarnby.
II23D-05.explanation: Sandoval credits installment plans, which dealers in both towns offered "only to buyers with a fixed salary, which clerks drew" and shopkeepers did not; Szabo credits conservatories, and only Sarnby had one. Clerks' and shopkeepers' households in Sarnby both had the conservatory, and the passage says the two groups' "incomes there were much alike," so the finding that "More clerks' households in Sarnby owned a piano than shopkeepers' households in Sarnby" isolates access to installment plans and most directly supports Sandoval. The finding that "More clerks' households in Sarnby owned a piano than shopkeepers' households in Thursk" compares households with both installment plans and a conservatory against households with neither, so Szabo's account predicts it as well. The finding that "More shopkeepers' households in Sarnby owned a piano than clerks' households in Thursk" has the group with a conservatory but no installment plans beating the group with installment plans but no conservatory, which weakens Sandoval. The finding that "More shopkeepers' households in Sarnby owned a piano than shopkeepers' households in Thursk" compares two groups without installment plans that differ only in the conservatory, so it supports Szabo and says nothing about installment plans.

II23D-06.correct_answer: the playhouse in Stennard drew 21,500 patrons in 1900.
II23D-06.explanation: Westergaard's claim needs a playhouse "with fewer than 400 seats" whose attendance "more than doubled" between 1890 and 1900. The table shows that Stennard has 320 seats and that its attendance rose from 9,800 to 21,500, about 2.2 times as many, so "the playhouse in Stennard drew 21,500 patrons in 1900." supports the claim. All four choices read the table accurately. Tavisholm's attendance rose from 11,200 to 26,300, more than doubling (about 2.3 times), but Tavisholm has 610 seats, so it is not a small playhouse. Ulvercote has 380 seats, but its attendance rose from 17,900 to 33,400, about 1.9 times, short of doubling. Varrick has 350 seats and drew the most patrons of the four in 1900, but its attendance rose from 24,600 to 41,800, only about 1.7 times.

II23D-07.correct_answer: Tarnside drew 3,900 visitors and sold 58 paintings.
II23D-07.explanation: Sorrell's example must draw "fewer than 20 visitors for each painting it showed" and sell "more than a quarter of its paintings." The table shows that Tarnside showed 210 paintings, so its 3,900 visitors come to about 18.6 per painting, and its 58 sales are about 27.6 percent of 210; "Tarnside drew 3,900 visitors and sold 58 paintings." meets both conditions. All four choices read the table accurately. Uxley's 84 sales are 26.25 percent of its 320 paintings, more than a quarter, but its 7,400 visitors come to about 23.1 per painting. Yoxholt drew about 17.9 visitors per painting (5,200 for 290), but its 69 sales are only about 23.8 percent. Velmont drew about 20.6 visitors per painting (3,700 for 180) and sold about 22.8 percent of its paintings (41 of 180), so it meets neither condition.

II23D-08.correct_answer: Vardleigh, which had 6 bookshops and 2 printing presses.
II23D-08.explanation: Thorne's example must be a town without a grammar school (the passage says "only Sedgeholm and Tolbridge had a grammar school") that had "at least one bookshop or printing press for every 1,200 residents." Vardleigh had no grammar school, and the table shows 9,400 residents for its 6 bookshops and 2 presses, 8 businesses in all, or one for every 1,175 residents; "Vardleigh, which had 6 bookshops and 2 printing presses." completes the text. All four choices read the table accurately. Sedgeholm had 5 businesses for 5,200 residents, one for every 1,040, but it had a grammar school. Wickerby, with no grammar school, had the most bookshops and presses, but its 15 businesses served 19,800 residents, one for every 1,320.
